items.summary_raw:
Though the climate talks officially finished on Friday, no final deal was agreed. NGOs are warning that this summit might fall disastrously short of what is needed

Although not quite deserted, the halls of the Cop31 conference centre are considerably less peopled today. A few people wander back and forth with their backpacks on. Young Turkish support staff walk around in groups.

It’s possible to find a seat at the tables next to the food stalls. Those, however, are closed, so there is nothing to actually rest on the table except for your laptop.

items.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
items.summary_raw:
Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

  • Cop31 live – latest updates

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

The sweeping bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (or Baaja), is now set for passage in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives before being signed by Donald Trump, who has claimed it will boost economic activity and lower energy costs.

On a rainy September morning, the Pamela Ann, a rusty, 86ft (26-metre) scallop boat, docked in New Bedford, Massachusetts. Its crew had spent the past 12 days at sea, recording mammal sightings, monitoring vessels to ensure they didn’t enter construction zones, and keeping watch over workers at Revolution Wind, a 65-turbine offshore wind project just south of Rhode Island.

“God forbid, if anybody was to fall, we could be there to help them out,” said Capt Kevin Souza, who has a bulldog tattoo on his shin to mark his time in the navy.

items.title: How the war in Iran turned the Gulf into a climate catastrophe – video explainer
items.summary_raw:
The war between the US, Israel and Iran has turned the strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes, into a battlefield, but also the centre of a deepening environmental disaster. Tankers struck by missiles or sea mines are leaking oil into the Gulf, leaving vast slicks visible from space, staining coastlines and threatening lasting damage to marine ecosystems. Many of these areas remain inaccessible because of the naval blockade, making it virtually impossible to document the devastation on the ground. The Guardian has examined dozens of satellite images and spoken to environmental experts in an effort to assess the scale of the damage

items.summary_raw:
The latest draft text has been published, as negotiations continue at the UN summit in Turkey

Ethiopia can show that taking strong action to solve the climate crisis can go along with economic growth in the developing world, the president-designate of next year’s Cop has said.

“Climate action and development and progress are not mutually exclusive,” Gedion Timothewos told the Guardian in an interview at Cop31. “Good economic policy, that has a positive impact on people’s pockets, and on GDP and your economy, can also be good climate action. That is something we believe the Ethiopian experience can showcase.”

Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems.

items.title: Cop31 live: rich world offering ‘crumbs’ to help poor countries adapt to climate breakdown, campaigners say
items.summary_raw:
Wealthy polluters promised to put $50m into an adaptation fund this week, less than half of what countries promised at last year’s climate summit

California Governor Gavin Newsom was a big presence in Antalya last week, serving as the head of a US delegation that attended unofficially due to President Donald Trump’s withdrawal from the international summit.

Widely seen as a top presidential contender for 2028, Newsom’s strong rhetoric in support of a fossil fuel phase out and other top climate priorities inspired hope that there’s a future for the US – the world’s second biggest emitter – in negotiations. That of course, depends on who ends up as the next resident of the White House, but Newsom made big promises regardless, as the head of California – the world’s fourth largest economy.

items.title: UK backs idea of new levies on polluting sectors to pay for climate action costs
items.summary_raw:
Britain joins other signatories to statement urging introduction of targeted taxes on heavy emitters

The UK has signed a statement that backs levies on polluting sectors to pay for the impacts of the climate crisis, in a strong political signal that could pave the way for frequent flyer and crypto taxes.

Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

items.title: Cop31 live: first draft of agreement under pressure as climate negotiations enter final days
items.summary_raw:
Thorny divisions emerge as wide-ranging draft deal seeks to ‘draw out parties’ on areas of disagreement

Speaking at a press conference just now, the EU’s climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, lamented the language on climate finance, trade and carbon capture (CCS) in the draft decision. He argued that the focus of this Cop was supposed to be on implementation. “It had the characteristics of a shopping list,” he said of yesterday’s text.

“That, in our view, is fundamentally at odds with the logic of implementation,” he added. “Delivering what we have already agreed on, that should be the focus. And that is why we do think that – particularly in the domain of finance, particularly in the domain of trade, also in the domain of CCS, and suggesting that might be the solution to everything – I think the cover decision does not go in the right direction and needs significant change.”

items.title: Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep | Miatta Fahnbulleh
items.summary_raw:
I am at Cop31 – concerned about the crisis around the world, but mindful that voters want jobs, warmer homes and cheaper prices

  • Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero

In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.

That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. items.title: What do you want to know about the Cop31 climate talks? Ask Fiona Harvey and Ajit Niranjan
items.summary_raw:
The Guardian’s environment editor Fiona Harvey and Europe environment correspondent Ajit Niranjan will answer your questions on Cop31, the draft deal on fossil fuels, the fight over climate finance and what overshooting 1.5C means for the world.

Ask a question: log in or sign up here

The Cop31 climate summit in Antalya is in its final days, and negotiators are fighting over a first draft of the deal.

It calls for “accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”, and for tripling adaptation finance for poorer countries. But with the world heading past the 1.5C limit and countries deeply divided over finance, adaptation and the “just transition”, can Cop31 deliver anything that matters?

Many countries surprised to see first version delivered with more than four days of negotiation remaining

A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.

Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.

Afin de garantir la confidentialité de cette présence militaire française dans un pays en guerre, il a été décidé, selon plusieurs sources proches du dossier avec qui RFI s’est entretenue, de s’appuyer sur la mission Gerfaut. Cette dernière, officiellement assumée, est un détachement militaire français présent en Pologne depuis février 2023 (notamment sur le camp de Wedrzyn, au nord-ouest de la Pologne) dans le cadre de la mission européenne EUMAM-Ukraine, prorogée pour une nouvelle période de deux ans, jusqu'au 15 novembre 2028.  🔴 URGENT -  Mission «Volia»: comment l'armée française opère en Ukraine ➡️ https://go.rfi.fr/vqH https

items.title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?
items.summary_raw:
Along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, its intertidal flats host a wealth of marine life and birds. But extraction industries, tourism and fishing are taking their toll

Stand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats.

As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world, this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009.

Aerial view of the unique features of the Wadden Sea coast. Photograph: Janis Meyer/CWSS

items.title: Choking fires, deadly heat and devastating floods: 2026 in extreme weather
items.summary_raw:
People around the world have contended with unprecedented weather events and their fatal effects caused by the climate catastrophe

After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.

As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.

items.title: Canada invests billions in charging infrastructure and grid upgrades
items.summary_raw: The Canadian government is investing in the expansion of electric vehicle charging and grid infrastructure with investments of just over $634 million. The new investment should roughly double the more than 50,000 chargers supported through existing programs. The EV charging initiative is further supported by the government’s national electricity strategy with over $50 billion to be invested in doubling the capacity of Canada’s grid by 2050.
